newsitem.title: USA: Hamas leader says deal struck to go to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader says deal struck to go to Jordan.

text.p: The leader of the political wing of the Palestinian group Hamas said on Thursday he believed a deal had been struck to send him to Jordan after Israel dropped its bid to extradite him.

Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook, a long-time resident of the United States, told Reuters in an interview in the New York prison where he has been held without charge or trial since July 1995 that the Israeli government's announcement had not surprised him.
"I knew they would never extradite me," said the soft-spoken Abu Marzook, who was arrested in July 1995 after his name was found on the U.S. list of people with suspected ties to terrorism.

"My understanding is that everything is done," he said, referring to the apparent agreement that he would be deported to Jordan, the country that asked him to leave in 1995 under pressure from Israel.
In Washington, however, U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno told reporters that the 47-year-old Palestinian political activist would remain in U.S. custody.
"It is in the INS (Immigration and Naturalisation Service) process, and we are reviewing all of our options." She said a "detainer" had been filed to keep him in a U.S. jail.

Abu Marzook said in the interview, in a visiting room of the Manhattan Correctional Centre, that a Jordanian official had gone to his family home in Virginia in recent days and told his wife that King Hussein was "doing his best" to arrange for his transfer to Jordan.
"I think they are going to do something before Monday," said Abu Marzook, who was relaxed and dressed in a prison-issue orange jumpsuit.
Asked whether he believed he would be freed from jail and sent to Jordan before a court hearing scheduled on Monday, he said: "Yes, this is my expectation."

Abu Marzook gave up his appeal against the extradition in January. Israel announced earlier on Thursday it was suspending its 18-month-old request for reasons "relating to security and the prevention of terrorism."

Israel alleged that the Palestinian was responsible as the head of Hamas's political wing for attacks that killed scores of Israelis, but did not contend that he personally committed any acts of violence.

Abu Marzook has denied involvement in any violence but he and his group oppose the 1993 accords signed by Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation leader Yasser Arafat, which created the self-ruling Palestinian Authority in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.

He was arrested at John F. Kennedy international airport as he arrived in the United States -- where he had lived for more than a decade as a student and businessman -- after immigration officials found his name on the U.S. government's "watch list" of people with "known or suspected ties to terrorist activities."
Abu Marzook has maintained that the U.S. documents issued to him, his wife and their six children were in order when he arrived back in the country.

His attorney had argued in court two days ago that federal law required the U.S. government to surrender him to Israel no later than March 28, but prosecutors said the deadline under a two-month limitation that began when Abu Marzook dropped his appeal was April 6.
